questions.q: What is the correct HTML syntax to link an external stylesheet named `styles.css` located in the same folder as the HTML file?
questions.a: `<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">` placed inside the `<head>` element. A wrong answer like `<style src="styles.css"></style>` or `<script src="styles.css"></script>` reveals confusion between the `<link>` tag (for external resources) and `<style>`/`<script>` tags (for embedded code). Students often mix up `href` vs `src` or forget `rel="stylesheet"`.

questions.q:
A developer writes `

Welcome

` and also has an internal stylesheet rule `h1 { color: blue; }`. What color will the heading be, and why?
questions.a: Red. Inline styles have higher specificity than internal (or external) stylesheet rules, so they override them regardless of order. A wrong answer of "blue" shows the student doesn't understand the specificity hierarchy: inline > internal/embedded > external. They may think "last declared wins" applies universally, not realizing inline styles sit at the top of the cascade for that element.

questions.q: You are styling a 5-page website where all pages share the same header, footer, and navigation bar, but each page has a unique hero section. Which CSS inclusion strategy minimizes duplication and maximizes maintainability?
questions.a: Use an external stylesheet (`common.css`) for shared components (header, footer, nav) and internal `<style>` blocks on each page for the unique hero section. A wrong answer like "put everything in one external file" creates unnecessary HTTP requests for page-specific styles, while "use inline styles for hero sections" sacrifices maintainability. The student must balance reuse (external) vs. scope isolation (internal).

questions.q: Compare the browser caching behavior of internal CSS vs. external CSS when a user navigates from `index.html` to `about.html` on the same site. Which reduces bandwidth on the second page load and why?
questions.a: External CSS reduces bandwidth because the browser caches `styles.css` after the first request and reuses it on `about.html` without re-downloading. Internal CSS is re-sent with every HTML page since it's embedded in each document. A wrong answer claiming "both cache equally" ignores that HTML documents are rarely cached aggressively, while static `.css` files are cached by default with long max-age headers.

questions.q: Critique this approach: "For a React component library, we'll put all styles in external CSS files and use BEM naming to avoid conflicts." Identify one scenario where this fails and suggest a better alternative.
questions.a: Fails when components need dynamic styles based on props (e.g., `<Button variant="primary" />` changing colors). External CSS + BEM can't express runtime values. Better: use CSS Modules or CSS-in-JS (styled-components) for component-scoped dynamic styling, keeping global theme tokens in external CSS. A weak answer misses the static-vs-dynamic distinction and suggests "just add more classes" which doesn't scale for arbitrary prop combinations.

questions.q: Design a 3-page portfolio site structure (HTML + CSS files) showing exactly where inline, internal, and external CSS each live. Annotate each choice with a one-line justification.
questions.a:
Expected structure:
- `index.html`, `projects.html`, `contact.html` each link `<link rel="stylesheet" href="global.css">` (external — shared layout, typography, colors)
- `projects.html` has `<style>` block for project-grid animations (internal — page-specific interactive behavior)
- `contact.html` has `<button style="background: #ff6b6b;">` on the submit button (inline — one-off emphasis color not reused)
A poor answer puts everything in one file or uses inline for repeated patterns, showing no grasp of scope-based separation.
